analysis.one_liner: Phases out direct federal student lending and routes all student loans through private banks and guaranty agencies.
analysis.headline: The Student Loan Privatization Act of 1995, which would have repealed the federal Direct Student Loan Program and sold off its loans to private buyers, died in the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended the Direct Student Loan Program, created in 1993, under which the federal government lends student loan money directly to borrowers. Instead, every student loan would again flow through the guaranteed-loan system, in which private banks make the loans, guaranty agencies insure them against default, and the federal government pays the guarantees and subsidies. The bill would cap direct lending at 40% of new loan volume for one year, then repeal the program entirely, force the sale of the government's direct-loan portfolio at auction, and send the proceeds to the Treasury [S2][S3]. It never got past its committee referral [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Private student loan lenders, guaranty agencies, and loan servicing companies, who would regain the entire federal student loan market once the government's direct lending program was repealed. Schools and borrowers would deal only with the guaranteed-loan system. The bill's findings argue private lenders deliver better efficiency and technology than federal administration [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Direct Student Loan Program effective October 1, 1997, and limits it to no more than 40% of new student loan volume for academic year 1995-1996 and zero thereafter, shifting all lending to the Federal Family Education Loan Program [S2][S3].

It amends the guaranty agency reserve rules so reserves recovered by agencies are not clawed back except in limited cases, and requires recovered funds to go to the Treasury for debt reduction rather than back to agency operations [S2][S3].

It directs the Education Secretary to auction off the outstanding direct-loan portfolios in sales of at least $40 million, sold without federal default guarantees, with proceeds returned to the Treasury [S2][S3].
It revises federal budget accounting for direct loans to include administrative costs, on the argument that earlier rules projected savings unlikely to materialize [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Student borrowers, who would lose the option of borrowing directly from the federal government and be routed through private lenders whose profits depend on federal guarantee payments and subsidies; and taxpayers, who fund the guarantee subsidies paid to banks and guaranty agencies in place of direct government lending.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the direct lending program outright rather than letting the two systems compete, removing the borrowing and repayment option that the 1993 law created [S2][S3].

Its savings case rests on accounting assumptions: the bill's own findings concede the core claim is that prior budget scoring of direct lending was inaccurate, not that guaranteed lending is demonstrably cheaper for borrowers [S3].

Selling the direct-loan portfolios without federal guarantees transfers servicing of existing borrowers' loans to private buyers on the terms of the original promissory notes, with no further federal regulation of those loans under the act [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's claimed benefits are administrative savings and private-sector efficiency, but its concrete effect is to hand the entire federal student loan market back to banks and guaranty agencies that earn fees and guarantee payments on every loan. Borrowers lose the direct, government-run alternative that was created partly to compete with the guaranteed-loan system. The auction of existing loans returns some money to the Treasury, but the loans are sold stripped of federal guarantees, leaving the buyers free to service them under the original note terms. The design reads as a Windfall for the guaranteed-loan industry more than a verified saving for students or taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 1995 and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. Daniel Coats of Indiana, joined by three Republican cosponsors including Sen. Judd Gregg, introduced the bill on August 11, 1995 [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day; that was the bill's last action [S5].
The committee never reported the bill, and no vote was ever held in either chamber before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, student borrowers kept the option of borrowing directly from the federal government and taxpayers kept the direct-lending channel rather than paying guaranteed-loan subsidies to private intermediaries. Banks and guaranty agencies did not regain exclusive control of federal student lending.

for.name: Sen. Daniel Coats
for.role: U.S. Senator from Indiana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Student Loan Privatization Act of 1995 and delivered introductory remarks

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Hampshire; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, named as an original sponsor at introduction

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Senate committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: The direct lending program was a signature administration initiative, and the administration opposed repeal efforts during the 1995-96 budget fights

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter in the record was a Republican — the sponsor and three cosponsors, all from the GOP — and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill [S4].

industries.industry: Student loan lenders and guaranty agencies (banks, Sallie Mae-style secondary markets, state guaranty agencies)
industries.note: The bill would repeal the government's direct lending program and make the guaranteed-loan system the only federal student loan channel, restoring lenders' and guaranty agencies' fee and guarantee revenue on every loan. Their income depends on federal guarantee payments, so eliminating the cheaper direct alternative protects their market rather than lowering borrowers' costs.

industries.industry: Federal direct-loan servicing workforce and contractors
industries.note: The bill caps direct-loan administrative funds at $50 million in 1996 and $45 million in 1997, then nothing, and bars system upgrades, eliminating the federal and contract workforce that runs direct lending. The bill's findings claim this involves 500 federal employees and over 15,000 contract employees [S3].
